opus-5.5.text:
That's a fun question, because I think about it from the researcher's side more often than the investor's side.

If I were writing checks, I'd be looking for teams that are honest about where the technology actually is today, not where the demo video makes it look. A lot of robotics startups right now are raising on the promise of general-purpose humanoids doing everything in your home. That's an exciting long-term vision, and I do believe we'll get there, but the gap between a curated demo and a robot that works reliably for thousands of hours in messy real-world environments is enormous.

So the first thing I'd want is a team that has picked a concrete wedge: a specific task in a specific setting where a robot can deliver real value now, even if it's only 90 or 95 percent reliable, and where there's a human in the loop or some kind of graceful fallback for the remaining cases. Think warehouse picking of particular item categories, lab automation, certain kinds of inspection or kitting. Places where the customer is already paying for labor that's hard to hire for.

Second, I'd look closely at the data strategy. In the learning-based era of robotics, the real moat isn't so much the hardware or even the model architecture, since those ideas spread quickly. It's whether the company has a flywheel: once robots are deployed, do they generate data that makes the next version better, and does that improvement compound? A startup that can collect diverse, high-quality interaction data at scale, whether through deployment, teleoperation, or clever use of human video, is in a much stronger position than one that's just fine-tuning someone else's foundation model on a small dataset.

Third, I'd care about the hardware being good enough and cheap enough, not perfect. Some teams over-engineer the hardware and burn their runway before they learn what the customer actually needs. Others neglect it and end up with robots that break constantly in the field. The sweet spot is a team with real full-stack experience, people who have taken a robot out of the lab and kept it running.

And finally, the people. Robotics is a long game. Things will take longer than the plan says, almost always. So I'd want founders who are deeply technical, but also patient and stubborn in the right way, who've already been humbled by real-world deployment and still want to keep going.

So to sum it up: a focused application with clear value today, a data flywheel that gets stronger with scale, practical hardware, and a team that's been through the pain of making robots work outside the lab. That's what I'd bet on.

r001.rationale: The response calls general-purpose humanoids an exciting long-term vision, but does not identify progress toward human-like robot components as an investment reason.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss foundational robotics technology that may take five years or longer to deploy in a humanoid robot.

r003.rationale: The response favors a focused application with clear value today, but does not connect commercial viability to sustaining the pursuit of longer-term technological breakthroughs.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, if I were an investor, I'd want to put money into teams that are obsessed with a specific, boring, repetitive job and have actually stood in that environment for a long time. Not a team pitching a general-purpose humanoid that will do everything someday, but one that says, "We know exactly what happens at 3 a.m. in this warehouse, or on this hospital floor, or in this kitchen, and here is the one task we're going to own completely."

The reason is that robotics is still a business of margins and reliability more than it is a business of demos. A robot that works 90 percent of the time looks incredible in a video and is almost worthless in deployment, because somebody still has to stand next to it. So I'd look for teams that are honest about failure modes, that measure uptime and cost per task instead of counting likes on a clip, and that have a clear path from the first ten units to the first thousand.

I'd also want to see that they treat software and data as the real product. Hardware is necessary, but hardware alone commoditizes fast. The companies that win will be the ones whose robots get better every week because every deployment feeds back into the models and the operations stack. If a startup can show me a learning loop that compounds, and a customer who is already paying because the thing saves them real money, that's the one I'd write the check for.

And a smaller point, but I care about it: I'd back founders who have shipped something physical before. Robotics punishes people who have only lived in simulation. Someone who has debugged a cable harness in a cold warehouse understands the problem in a way that a pitch deck never shows.

r001.rationale: The response favors focused, task-specific robotics companies and does not identify progress toward human-like robot components as a long-term investment reason.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss foundational robotics technology that could be valuable despite lacking humanoid deployment within five years.

r003.rationale: The response emphasizes paying customers and commercial performance, but does not say commercial viability sustains the pursuit of longer-term technological breakthroughs.

astra-6.text:
I’d look for a robotics startup solving a very specific problem that customers are already paying to solve. Who needs this robot, what does it do for them, and why is it better than the alternative? That matters more to me than how impressive the demo looks.

I’d also pay close attention to the team’s ability to deploy it. Can the robot work reliably outside the lab? Can they manufacture it, maintain it, and make the economics work for the customer? A narrow application with a clear return on investment would be a compelling place to start. Then I’d want to understand how that first product gives them a path to something bigger.

r001.rationale: The response favors a clear application and a path to something bigger, but does not identify progress toward human-like robot components as a long-term investment reason.

r002.rationale: It does not state that foundational robotics technology can be valuable even if it cannot be deployed in a humanoid robot within five years.

r003.rationale: The response emphasizes customer return and a viable first product, but does not connect commercial viability to sustaining a startup’s pursuit of longer-term technological breakthroughs.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d look for a robotics startup solving a very specific problem that customers are already paying to solve. Who needs this robot, what does it do better, and does the economics make sense once you include deployment, maintenance, and human intervention?

I’d be especially interested in a team that can start with one useful task and learn from real deployments. In robotics, a great demo is only the beginning. Getting a system to work reliably every day in a customer’s environment is the hard part. So I’d invest in a team that understands both the technology and the operational details—and has customers willing to pay.

r001.rationale: The response discusses useful tasks and reliable deployment, but does not identify progress toward human-like robot components as a long-term investment reason.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss foundational robotics technology, humanoid robots, or the five-year deployment horizon.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes paying customers and sound economics, but does not connect commercial viability to sustaining a pursuit of longer-term technological breakthroughs.
